title: How to Forgive Someone Who Has Not Apologized
excerpt: Waiting for an apology that may never come hands the offender control of your healing. Forgiveness is something you can do without their permission.
body:
The hardest forgiveness is the kind no one asks you for. When someone wrongs you and then apologizes, forgiveness is still costly but it has a path. When someone wrongs you and never acknowledges it, never says sorry, maybe does not even think they did anything, you are left holding the whole weight alone, and every instinct says you are entitled to hold it until they make it right. I understand that instinct. I have nursed it. But waiting for an apology that may never come puts the offender in charge of your freedom, and that is a strange prison to choose, the one where the person who hurt you also keeps the key.

## Forgiveness is something you can do alone

Here is the freeing thing, and it took me years to believe it. Forgiveness does not require the other person's participation. It is, at its root, a decision you make before God to release a debt, to stop demanding the payment you are owed (Colossians 3:13). The offender does not have to be present, repentant, or even alive for you to forgive them. You are not waiting on them. You never were.

This is why Jesus could forgive from the cross people who were actively mocking him and had offered no apology. Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34). They had not asked. He did it anyway, because forgiveness is a posture of the heart toward the offender, not a transaction that requires their signature. You can begin it today, with no cooperation from anyone.

## What forgiveness is not

Let me clear away the things people confuse with forgiveness, because the confusion makes them refuse it. Forgiveness is not saying it did not matter; it mattered, which is exactly why it needs forgiving. It is not forgetting; you may remember it the rest of your life. It is not the absence of consequences; you can forgive a person and still not hand them your trust or your front door key. And it is not necessarily reconciliation. Reconciliation takes two people and a repaired trust; forgiveness takes one.

This matters enormously for the unrepentant offender. You can fully forgive someone and still keep a healthy distance from them, still refuse to pretend nothing happened, still decline to reenter a situation that harmed you. Forgiving the person who never apologized does not mean letting them hurt you again. It means releasing your claim on revenge while keeping your wisdom about safety.

## Why you cannot afford to hold it

When you refuse to forgive, you imagine you are punishing the offender, but they are usually living their life untroubled while the poison sits in you. Bitterness does not hurt the person it is aimed at. It hurts the person it lives in. Hebrews calls it a root of bitterness that springs up and defiles many (Hebrews 12:15), and the word picture is exact: it grows down into you, spreads, and poisons more than the original wound ever did.

Unforgiveness is also corrosive to your relationship with God, because the same parable where the unforgiving servant is condemned is the one Jesus tells about us (Matthew 18:21-35). We who have been forgiven an unpayable debt cannot clutch the small debts owed to us without something going wrong in us. Holding it does not protect you. It deforms you.

## How to actually do it

Forgiveness is usually not a single moment but a decision you make and then keep remaking. Name the wrong specifically before God, the actual thing, not a vague haze. Say plainly what you are releasing: I forgive this person this debt, and I give up my right to repay them. Then, when the memory returns and the anger flares again, as it will, forgive again. Seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22) is not just about repeated offenses; it is also about the same offense you have to keep releasing as it keeps surfacing.

Pray for the person, which Jesus commands and which is nearly impossible at first and slowly becomes possible (Matthew 5:44). You cannot stay bitter toward someone you are genuinely asking God to bless. The prayer changes you long before it changes anything else, and changing you was always the point.

## This week

Name the specific wrong and the person who never apologized. Say out loud to God that you release the debt, that you give up the apology you are owed and the revenge you crave. When the bitterness rises again this week, do it again. Begin praying for that person, even badly, even reluctantly.

The apology may never come. Your freedom does not depend on it. Forgiveness is the one thing in this whole situation you can do without anyone's permission, and it is the thing that gets you out of the prison you did not choose.
